titleDark.text: Dark mode — same screens, same components, tokens switched

titlePlan.text: Plan & track — Timeline, Calendar, Workload, Sprints

ux6.text:
UX decisions — Timeline

1. Task list on the left, bars on the right share one row height, so the eye tracks across (Gestalt continuity).

2. Dependencies are drawn as connectors; the critical path is the only thing in brand blue (Von Restorff).

3. A dashed baseline under each bar shows plan vs actual without a second chart.

4. Milestones are diamonds — a shape everyone reads as a point in time (Jakob’s Law).

5. The Today line and Day / Week / Month / Quarter zoom keep orientation. Drag a bar edge to reschedule; dependents shift with an Undo toast.

6. A conflict (task starting before its blocker ends) gets a warning badge, not a blocked action (Error prevention).

ux7.text:
UX decisions — Calendar

1. Month grid with task chips colored by project dot + status icon, never color alone.

2. Today is the only filled date marker.

3. Busy days collapse to “+3 more” (Miller’s Law) and open a popover, so cells never grow uneven.

4. Unscheduled tasks sit in a side tray — drag them onto a day to schedule (direct manipulation).

5. Week and Day views share the same chips and drag behavior (Consistency).

ux8.text:
UX decisions — Workload

1. One row per person, one cell per day: hours planned vs capacity.

2. Load uses a lightness scale AND a number in every cell; over capacity adds a warning icon (colorblind-safe).

3. Time off is hatched, so it never reads as “free”.

4. Summary chips at the top answer the PM’s question first: who is overloaded this week?

5. Drag a task from an overloaded cell to someone with space; the AI suggestion proposes a rebalance you can accept or ignore.

ux9.text:
UX decisions — Sprint

1. Sprint header shows the goal, dates and days left — the context for every decision below.

2. Burndown: ideal line dashed, actual line solid, scope change marked. One chart, one message: are we on pace?

3. Capacity bar warns when committed points exceed the team’s average velocity (Error prevention).

4. Backlog is ranked; drag into the sprint or press Shift+S. Estimates are always visible to keep planning honest.

5. “Complete sprint” leads to the retrospective with unfinished work pre-sorted (Tesler’s Law).

ux10.text:
UX decisions — Inbox

1. Tabs: Mentions, Assigned, Approvals — the three kinds of “needs me”.

2. Each item says who, what and where in one line, with the quoted context below (Recognition over recall).

3. Unread is a blue dot + bold title, not color alone.

4. Approvals can be done inline: Approve / Request changes, no navigation.

5. Keyboard triage: E archive, H snooze, U mark unread, ↵ open. Bulk select with X.

6. Snoozed items return at the chosen time; archive is undoable.

ux11.text:
UX decisions — Dashboard

1. KPI tiles first: the number, the change, and what “good” means (Visibility of system status).

2. Every chart answers one question in its title (“Are we finishing what we start?”).

3. Colorblind-safe palette; series are labeled directly, no legend hunting.

4. Project health table: icon + label + color, sortable, links to each project.

5. Edit layout, Share and Schedule email live in the header; widgets are drag-to-arrange in edit mode only (progressive disclosure).

ux12.text:
UX decisions — Members & roles

1. Roles explained in plain words next to the picker; the permission matrix is one click away, not on the main screen (progressive disclosure).

2. Pending invites are listed with Resend / Revoke so nothing is a dead end.

3. Guests are visually separated and limited by default (security by default).

4. Deactivate is reversible and keeps the person’s work; only Delete asks for confirmation.

5. SSO / SCIM status is shown up top for admins so they know where people come from.

ux13.text:
UX decisions — Billing & plan limit

1. Usage meters for seats, storage, automations and AI credits — limits are visible before they are hit (no surprise walls).

2. The limit prompt shows what the locked feature does and lets you preview it (contextual upgrade).

3. Monthly / annual toggle shows the saving in money, not just a percentage.

4. One recommended plan is highlighted (Von Restorff); the rest are comparable at a glance.

5. Downgrade and cancel are always reachable — with a pause option and data export, never hidden.

ux14.text:
UX decisions — Mobile

1. Bottom tab bar: Home, My tasks, Inbox, Search — thumb reach (Fitts’s Law). Create is a floating + button.

2. Rows are 56px with 44×44 targets; text is 16px.

3. Swipe right to complete, left to snooze, with an icon revealed under the finger and an Undo toast.

4. Task detail is a full screen with the same properties as desktop, in the same order (Consistency).

5. Inbox triage is one item at a time with large Approve / Archive buttons; push notifications deep-link straight here.

ux1.text:
UX decisions — My tasks

1. Greeting + one-line summary answers “what needs me today?” before any scanning (Visibility of system status). Dates are human: Today, 2 days ago.

2. Grouped by due date, Overdue first. Only overdue uses red, so it is the one thing that pops (Von Restorff, Serial Position, Miller’s Law).

3. List / Board / Calendar are tabs that keep filters; “My focus” is a saved view (Flexibility & efficiency, Recognition over recall).

4. Inline quick-add with @ assign, # project, ! priority; C works anywhere (Tesler’s Law, keyboard-first).

5. Completing is optimistic with an 8s Undo toast instead of a confirm dialog (User control & freedom, Doherty Threshold).

6. “Getting started 3 of 5” stays in the sidebar until done (Zeigarnik Effect).

ux2.text:
UX decisions — Project board

1. Health is icon + label + color, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1).

2. “3 / 4 WIP” turns amber near the column limit and warns before it is exceeded (Error prevention).

3. The dragged card tilts with a stronger shadow; a dashed drop zone shows exactly where it lands (figure-ground). Keyboard: M “Move to…”, Alt+←/→.

4. Overview, List, Board, Timeline, Calendar, Workload are tabs on one project with shared filters (Consistency, Jakob’s Law).

5. Done cards recede; the next column peeks at the edge to signal horizontal scroll.

6. Up to four avatars, then +3 (Miller’s Law); hover shows names.

ux3.text:
UX decisions — Task detail panel

1. A side panel, not a new page: the list stays visible and the selected row is highlighted. Esc closes, ↗ opens full page.

2. Autosave with a quiet “Saved” — no Save button (Visibility of system status, optimistic UI with rollback).

3. Label → value grid; every value edits inline on click. Due today turns red with an icon.

4. “Blocked by” sits in the properties, not buried in activity (Error prevention).

5. AI output is labeled, names its source, and needs Add / Edit / Discard — AI never writes silently.

6. Subtask progress + AI “Break down” (Zeigarnik, Tesler).

7. The comment composer is pinned; @ mentions, ⌘↵ sends (Fitts’s Law).

Narrow list: tag and due columns hide automatically.

ux4.text:
UX decisions — Command palette

1. One box to search, act and navigate (Flexibility & efficiency). The scope chip narrows results without a new screen.

2. Natural language goes to AI first: “overdue design” becomes a ready filter.

3. Results stay in ≤ 4 groups (Hick’s Law) and every row shows its shortcut, so the palette teaches shortcuts.

4. Fuzzy matching runs locally in under 50ms; server results stream in after (Doherty Threshold).

5. Focus is trapped, arrows move the highlight, Esc returns focus to the trigger (WCAG 2.1.2, 2.4.3).

ux5.text:
UX decisions — First-run home

1. One highlighted next step — Invite 2 teammates — with the reason it matters (Von Restorff). Inviting is the team “aha” moment.

2. Checklist with visible progress; done steps stay struck through for closure (Zeigarnik, Peak-End).

3. The empty state explains what will appear, offers a primary action and an alternative (Import). Never a blank screen.

4. Templates beat the blank page (Tesler’s Law, Jakob’s Law). Target: first task in under 5 minutes.

5. “?” opens the shortcut sheet (Help & documentation).
